title: Lineage-Switch-on-a-Chip: A PRESS Framework  for Reconstructing and Validating Immunotherapy-Driven Cell-Fate Escape in Acute Leukemia
content: Antigen-directed immunotherapy has created an evolutionary pressure in acute leukemia that conventional drug-resistance models were never designed to reproduce. Lineage switch represents its most radical manifestation: a leukemia escapes therapy not merely by losing a target antigen but by changing developmental identity while retaining evidence of malignant clonal continuity. Project EVOLVE identified 75 post-immunotherapy lineage-switch cases, including 53 B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL)-to-acute myeloid leukemia (AML) transformations and 17 B-ALL-to-mixed-phenotype or ambiguous-lineage transformations. Among the 70 principal B-ALL cases, lineage switch emerged after a median of 1.5 months, 64.3% carried KMT2A rearrangements, and median survival after switch was only 4.8 months. Human bone-marrow organoids, leukemia-on-chip platforms, and immunocompetent microphysiological systems can now reproduce stromal interactions, vascular trafficking, immune killing, therapeutic resistance, and relapse, but these capabilities do not by themselves establish cell-fate conversion. This Review defines the lineage-switch-competent model and introduces the PRESS framework: Pressure, Reconstruction, Evolution, State transition, and Stability. It further introduces LSCM-MINIMUM, a set of proposed and falsifiable evidentiary criteria requiring malignant clonal continuity, multidimensional lineage reassignment, longitudinal capture of transition, no detectable pre-existing independent alternate-lineage clone at the stated analytical sensitivity, a demonstrable relationship to defined therapeutic pressure, and persistence of the alternate state. Neither PRESS nor LSCM-MINIMUM is presented as a validated consensus standard; both are intended as testable frameworks for experimental refinement. The defining endpoint of a lineage-switch model is not survival after therapy, antigen loss, or acquisition of an alternate-lineage marker; it is longitudinally demonstrated cell-fate transition within a genetically continuous malignant clone. Establishing that standard could convert lineage switch from a retrospective clinical observation into a tractable experimental mechanism and, ultimately, a preventable mode of relapse.
